reply: For a pilot you can start with two simple NIR concepts – transmission for the clear whey and diffuse‑reflection for the opaque milk concentrate – and run a side‑by‑side comparison against your lab protein/fat results.

report.title: Pilot measurement concepts for whey (clear) and milk concentrate (opaque)

answer.text: It depends on the optical appearance: NIR transmission is suited to the clear whey, while NIR diffuse‑reflection works for the opaque concentrate.

concept.summary: Install a transmission NIR probe in the whey line (optical path 1–5 mm) and a diffuse‑reflection NIR probe in the concentrate line (back‑scatter geometry). Both probes connect via low‑OD silica fiber to a high‑speed diode‑array NIR analyzer; calibration models are built from lab‑measured protein/fat data.

The key experimental action is the precise control of the optical pathlength (usually 1 - 10 mm); if the pathlength is too wide, the signal is lost to absorption; if too narrow, the sample represents a negligible volume.

risks: Transmission probe may saturate if concentrate is sampled; ensure pathlength control.
Reflection probe may be sensitive to surface fouling; requires regular cleaning.
Calibration models may not transfer directly from lab cuvettes to in‑line probes without validation.

steps: Collect representative whey and concentrate samples in the lab.
Measure each with the chosen NIR probes and with reference protein/fat assays.
Build separate chemometric calibration models (e.g., PLS) for protein and fat.
Validate each model on held‑out samples and assess prediction error.
Install probes in pilot‑scale loops and repeat the measurement‑comparison experiment to confirm in‑line performance.
feasibility.decisionBasis: If the validation RMSEP meets the detection limits (once defined) and the measurement latency satisfies the process requirement, the method is deemed feasible.

premiseChecks.detail: The medium changes from clear to opaque, so a single transmission path may saturate. Plan ATR or reflection for the opaque phase, or check the path length on samples from both phases.

assumptions: The whey is sufficiently clear for NIR transmission (optical density low).
